children.author: swyx
children.text:
i'm on a performance grind rn so also looked into it. claudeslop disclaimer below:

Hacker Books painted in 0.48 seconds on a fresh mobile visit. The first book cards were in the DOM by 0.79 seconds, and the largest visible image painted at 1.52 seconds. On a repeat visit, that image painted in 0.21 seconds.

Homepage median Fresh browser cache Repeat visit

First byte 112 ms 86 ms

First contentful paint 480 ms 168 ms

First book cards inserted 793 ms 188 ms

Largest contentful paint 1,520 ms 212 ms

Three runs per condition in Chrome at 390 × 844, with 1.6 Mbps download, 120 ms emulated latency and 4× CPU slowdown. These are navigation-start lab timings from one location. All three fresh visits beat your 1.5-second FCP target. Hacker Books

What makes it feel fast

- The first screen needs very little code. The HTML is about 3 KB, its single blocking stylesheet 5 KB, and its vanilla JavaScript module 26 KB, all gzip-compressed. The HTML contains the header, search box and navigation, so those can paint before the catalog arrives. There’s no React runtime to download or hydrate.

- They publish a small answer to the first query. The homepage preloads a 33 KB index of the top 600 books alongside the app code. The full 692 KB index of 15,362 books loads in the background. Once it arrives, browsing and search can reuse it locally. Covers are 320 px WebPs, and additional cards render in batches as you scroll.

- A book click can show the title immediately. The app changes the URL hash, renders the book information already in memory, then fills in comments and related material from a per-book JSON file. Hovering or focusing a card for 80 ms starts that fetch early. Repeat visits reuse the result. This is targeted data prefetching; it costs much less than prerendering an entire destination.

- Cloudflare helps on both visits. My HTML request was a cache HIT at Cloudflare’s San Jose edge. The versioned CSS, JS and index files advertise a one-year immutable browser cache. Chrome recorded zero transfer bytes for those files on all three repeat visits. HTTP/3 was real, too: two fresh visits negotiated H3 and one negotiated H2. All three painted within 468–500 ms, so the site was fast on either protocol in this sample.

- Open Graph handles sharing. The title, description and URL tags describe the site to link-preview crawlers. They don’t accelerate rendering. The page also includes Cloudflare Web Analytics.

The site is really fast. I see HTTP/3, OpenGraph, and Cloudflare. Can you expand on the technologies used?

Are you referring to the "Top all-time" list? That list seems to be mostly filled with popular books that do not go into too much detail, which is required for a decent treatment of probability and statistics.

There is a separate topic "Data & Statistics" that has quite some relevant titles.

Also, I think the interest in probability theory has only recently grown with the advent of generative AI. I'm expecting more interest in the future.

Edit: also, the site seems to miss some nice gems, most likely because they are not traditionally published books: "Probabilistic Artificial Intelligence" is freely available on Arxiv, and was discussed on Hacker News in March 2025 [1].

[1] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=43318624

You know, one thing that I think is interesting in tech circles is how much interest we have in maths in general, except that there is almost nothing on the "top" list that I saw that was related to probability and statistics. It's like P&S, which is probably the most useful math for most people who need to make decisions in life, is just not that interesting to people with a technical bend.

I wonder if it is because simulation can often allow you to get around needing P&S techniques in general? Or maybe it is that (Neural Network) ML models allow you to often approximate the things you might do with P&S in terms of making decisions?

No real point, I just think it is interesting.

Many life and work problems have relevant fiction books that cover similar or loosely related situations. Reading these can create a perfect “mental sandbox” for problem solving, where your brain unconsciously plays around with a topic in a safe and fun way, all while you’re following a fictional narrative.

This is an alternative to more “rational” methods, like reading non-fiction, prompting an LLM for possible approaches, or problem-solving explicitly. Brains work in weird ways, and they often need lots of unstructured time, lateral thinking, and play. Reading fiction provides all three.

I read a lot of non-fiction books when I was younger (during the whole improve-yourself trip of course) and most of them were so incredibly boring (always one concept explained with a 100 similar examples). children.text: I’ll add: re-read books. When reading a book a second time (or third, or fourth) you’ll get new things out of it because you’ll spend less time and energy focused on the obvious things you’re already familiar with. And if it’s been some good number of years I think you’ll also find your memory of the book isn’t as good as you might have thought.

children.author: chunky1994
children.text:
Whenever this topic comes up I always wonder if people mean reading as all long-form reading (including pop fiction) or if they mean “serious” reading. To me it’s actually quite strange but I feel like I have “lessened” as a reader over the past decades.

I used to be able to read some of the more classic novels a bit easier and now I just find them…a tad tedious? Is that the decline of reading that people are mentioning, or just… not reading at all?

I find it remarkably easy to read the popcorn fiction novels or anything very plot driven where characterization and world building is only in the service of the plot, but somehow this just feels like watching a movie but in book form. Is that also considered “reading”?

On the subject of reading (since the 'decline' in literacy is being raised in this thread) -- especially if you haven't read in a while and are thinking about reading but are maybe struggling to because you feel like it's "been too long" or that you'll struggle to concentrate on a book...

Please give reading (especially fiction) another chance. I had a stretch of about a decade where I finished maybe two or three books total. Partly, I didn't think I "needed to read" because of how much time I spend reading HN and other non-fiction sources, especially on the internet: or that I was "too busy".

I was running my startup, and had a copy of Infinite Jest on my bedside table for nearly 2 years -- telling myself that I would finish it. It's an amazing book (the part I've read anyway), but it was such an intricate piece of work that I managed to convince myself I basically had reading-ADHD and there was no point in me trying to read other books.

Last year, I started reading (fiction!) books that were just interesting to me or that other people were talking about, instead of picking up "aspirational" fiction or non-fiction and reading the first chapter.

I've been getting through a book every month or two since and am absolutely loving it. I read a lot of fiction as a child and teenager and I'd forgotten just how visceral good fiction can be. Reading properly again also helped convince me to write stories, too.

If this sounds like you, I challenge you (with kindness) to pick up a piece of approachable fiction and see how much more you get out of it than you expected to!

text:
Saw Karpathy's HackerTube and wanted the same thing for books. So I had Claude build one (Opus 5.5).

It's ~16.5k books that at least two different HN commenters brought up, from 2007 till now. Each book links back to the comments that mentioned it. Data is downloadable from the about page.

To be clear: Claude wrote almost all of it, including the data pipeline and the site. I mostly steered and made calls, bought the domain name, etc.

It counts mentions, so it's not perfect (praising a book and trashing it both count). If your favourite book is missing or matched to the wrong thing, tell me.
title: Show HN: HackerBooks – HackerTube, but for books mentioned on HN
